newsitem.title: UK: Britain's drought drains resources, boosts bets.
newsitem.headline: Britain's drought drains resources, boosts bets.

text.p: All bets are off for a dry April after a trace of rain was detected in London on Monday, British bookmakers William Hill said on Tuesday.
But the month is still on track to be the driest on record as Britain's long-running drought continues.
The Meteorological Office (Met) has so far recorded just one millimetre of rain in April, compared with a previous record low of eight millimetres in 1938 and below averages of 60 millimetres.
And Britons are expecting the national election on May 1 to be a dry day, with William Hill offering 6-4 on for no rain.
Punters can still get odds of 50-1 against a totally dry May and comparatively narrow odds of 25-1 that temperatures will reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit for the first time ever this summer.
But while punters and the public may be basking in the sunshine, the dry weather is causing headaches for Britain's water companies and farmers.
Ground water levels throughout the country are well below average, and in some parts have broken record lows.
Farmers in eastern England have been asked to cut back by up to 50 percent on the amount of water they take for spray irrigation. The Environment Agency said other areas should also take note.
"Everyone needs to be aware of water conservation," a spokesman said. "They should make careful use of a precious resource."
Britain endured its hottest summer ever in 1995 and has now seen its driest two years for over 200 years, with 360 millimetres less rain in the period than average.
Although reservoirs are largely near average capacities for the season, it is the level of groundwater -- natural reserves from rain seeping into the earth -- which is causing concern.
The Environment Agency said moisture in the soil was down in every region at the beginning of April with eastern England and the Thames-area around London worst hit.
But the region's water authority says it remains confident that it has enough resources for the summer and does not anticipate any bans on hosepipes to water the garden.

But the area, away from the country's prevailing westerly rain-carrying winds, is traditionally one of Britain's driest. "We are used to looking after what we have got carefully," the water authority said.
Water companies are moving to persuade customers to cut back on demand, introducing meters and producing information aimed at saving on domestic use.
But they are coming under increasing pressure to tackle leaks of water by lobby groups and the opposition Labour Party, which is riding ahead of the ruling Conservatives in the polls.
More than 800 million gallons of water a day seep out of pipes in Britain, and Labour has called for companies to introduce a crash programme immediately to mend leaks.

The Water Services Association, which represents the major water companies, argues that its members have invested heavily in pipes and nearly 100 million gallons a day are being saved since last year.
Whatever the immediate solutions, observers remain divided over the long-term prospects for Britain.
Some suggest the country is experiencing a dramatic shift in its climate, but the Met is sceptical.
"Even three years of excessively low rainfall could just be another extreme variation rather than a change, which has to be tracked over decades," a spokesman said.

The Met also thinks the first two weeks of May could see average or slightly above-average rainfall and bookmakers William Hill pointed out that Christmas Day last year was the first on record to see snow in London.
Whatever the weather, betting shops are likely to stay busy.
"Very volatile weather attracts more betting interest," the William Hill spokesman said, adding that the chain would have had to pay out six-figure sums if April had stayed dry.
